title: Pride in hillbilly roots and the fiddle breakdown repertoire of Cliff Gross
summary: The band wanted to leave the strings label but kept its fiddle breakdowns. Parker explains how Cliff Gross's catalogue was kept by copying the radio transcription records.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: In a funny kind of way. Yeah. All through this time though. Instrumentation. We had that same idea there from then. Did you ever want to get to the point where you could say, I'm no longer a hillbilly musician?
Oh, I guess maybe. This is why I wanted to go to school. I'm sure why all of us were trying to break the strings in a way.

If you had achieved this status, do you think that it would have been the kind of a thing where you would have at that point no longer been a hillbilly band? Or would you have always, I mean, in terms of your own attitudes, were you proud of this background that you wanted to bring up? Did you want to bring up the level of hillbilly or did you want to climb above the level of

hillbilly? No, I think we carried it all right with us because always the violinists who played this breakdown, and old Cecil Brower played Beaumont Rag. Mm-hmm. And all that business of the, yes, we carry that always. And we're proud of, there's a great deal of virtuosity really in playing the old, the Sailor's Horn by Durang's Reel and all those are sometimes quite difficult accomplishments really. And our violinists played superbly. We were proud of them. And they were the ones who played these old breakdowns, and we'd laugh and go right along.
How were these old fiddle breakdowns in the repertoire of the band?

They'd always been there. This Cecil, the first of Brower, no, Cliff Gross. Cliff Gross from Bowling Green, Kentucky had been the first one who played them. And whenever he left the band, we had to get ASCAP came in later on and we had to clear everything and clear all the breakdowns too. And we didn't know. He was the one who played all of them and we didn't know those. And when he left the band, he took with him his whole catalog and itinerary. But he had left, we used to make record every day. Every day we would make one record that would be made in triplicate by the recording engineer for the radio stations in Arkansas. And Gross had made years of these records and on these accumulations of records was his whole repertoire of breakdowns. And we simply, the violinist, Kenneth Fitz simply copied them all from the records and we had everything.
